content: A large study tracking more than 316,000 adults for up to 15 years suggests that a routine blood test may reveal important clues about future dementia risk. A standard blood test taken during a routine health check could offer clues about dementia risk more than a decade later. In a study of more than 316,000 adults, researchers found that people with unusually low or high levels of hemoglobin were more likely to develop dementia, although the risks varied depending on the type of disease. Hemoglobin is the oxygen-carrying protein in red blood cells. Low levels are commonly associated with anemia, while unusually high levels can result from smoking, dehydration, or certain heart and lung conditions. The findings suggest that this familiar blood measurement may also reflect broader aspects of physical health associated with brain aging. Researchers analyzed health records from 316,542 Korean adults aged 40 and older who underwent national health screenings in 2004 and 2005. Participants were divided into five groups based on their hemoglobin levels, from the lowest 20% to the highest 20%. National health insurance records were then used to track new dementia diagnoses through the end of 2019. Compared with the group that had the lowest dementia rate, participants in the lowest hemoglobin category had a 16% higher risk of developing dementia from any cause. Those in the highest category had a 7% greater risk. The findings, published in the Journal of Alzheimer’s Disease and presented at the 39th ECNP Congress in Munich, also identified differences between Alzheimer’s disease and vascular dementia. For Alzheimer’s disease, the increased risk was concentrated among people with the lowest hemoglobin levels. Participants in this group were 14% more likely to develop the disease than those in the reference group. The relationship was different for vascular dementia (caused by reduced blood flow to the brain). People in the lowest hemoglobin category had a 19% higher risk, while those in the highest category had an 18% higher risk. However, the association did not follow a consistent pattern across all five hemoglobin groups. The researchers also observed clearer and more consistent relationships among women than men. Lead researcher Dr. Hyun Soo Kim, an assistant professor at Dong-A University College of Medicine in Busan, South Korea, emphasized that the results do not establish a direct causal relationship. “The findings do not show that hemoglobin itself causes dementia, but suggest that abnormal hemoglobin levels may be a visible marker of wider physical vulnerability relevant to brain health.” Kim added, “Dementia is one of the fastest-growing health challenges in aging societies, and there are not many treatments and no cure. Identifying simple, accessible markers of future risk could help researchers and clinicians better understand how whole-body health relates to brain health over time.” Hemoglobin is already measured in standard blood tests around the world, making it considerably more accessible than specialized brain imaging or newer dementia biomarkers. The researchers suggest that existing blood test results could potentially help scientists investigate connections between general physical health and long-term cognitive decline. Kim explained, “A blood test most people already get at a routine check-up may say something about their brain health many years later. In this large Korean cohort, people with unusually low hemoglobin, and, to a smaller degree, those with unusually high hemoglobin, were more likely to develop dementia. This does not prove that hemoglobin causes dementia, but it supports the idea that general physical health, including the body’s ability to carry oxygen, matters for long-term brain health.” Because the study was observational, it cannot determine whether abnormal hemoglobin levels contribute directly to dementia. Other medical conditions could influence both hemoglobin measurements and brain health. Early dementia processes might also affect nutrition, body weight, frailty, or anemia before the disease is formally diagnosed. “We want to emphasize that the findings should not be interpreted as advice to take iron supplements, to raise hemoglobin levels, or to lower high hemoglobin levels in order to prevent dementia. An abnormal hemoglobin result should instead be discussed with a doctor, because it may point to underlying health issues that deserve attention,” Kim said. The study drew on health records from South Korea, leaving questions about whether the same relationships apply to people from other ethnic, geographic, and medical backgrounds. Further research is also needed to establish whether identifying abnormal hemoglobin levels can meaningfully improve dementia risk assessment or prevention. Dr. Lindsey Sinclair (University of Southampton), who was not involved in the research, commented: “There is a growing body of evidence that physical health and brain health are intertwined. We are also increasingly aware that changes supporting better brain health, be they medical or lifestyle changes, are important in mid-life to reduce the risk of later dementia. While this study shows a possible link between hemoglobin levels and dementia risk, more work is required to understand if this link is present in people from a wider range of backgrounds; and what can best be done to reduce dementia risk in people with the lowest and highest levels of hemoglobin.” Meeting: 39th ECNP Congress Never miss a breakthrough: Join the SciTechDaily newsletter. content: Laboratory experiments show that antibodies associated with childhood cancer can enter cells and bind DNA repair proteins, suggesting a possible route by which the immune system could weaken genetic safeguards. Years before some children were diagnosed with cancer, their blood already contained antibodies directed against proteins that normally repair damaged DNA. Researchers in Norway have found that these antibodies were much more common among children who later developed cancer than among those who did not, raising the possibility that the immune system itself may interfere with a cell’s ability to protect its genetic material. Childhood cancers, including leukemia, myeloma, neuroblastoma, and osteosarcoma, differ from adult cancers in their causes, locations, and responses to treatment. Children have had far less time to accumulate DNA damage from environmental exposures, lifestyle factors, and aging. Their tumors therefore tend to contain fewer mutations and often arise from immature cells, such as stem cells or progenitor cells that can develop into more specialized cell types. Cells rely on hundreds of proteins to identify and repair damage or errors in their DNA. The Norwegian researchers suspect that this protective machinery may sometimes be disrupted by auto-antibodies, antibodies that mistakenly target the body’s own proteins rather than foreign threats. If these antibodies interfere with DNA repair, genetic damage could accumulate even without inherited defects in the genes responsible for maintaining the genome. To investigate this possibility, Serguienko, Dr Ola Myklebost, and their colleagues analyzed the proteome, or collection of expressed proteins, in tumor and blood samples from 175 adults and children with sarcoma or acute lymphoblastic leukemia. The samples were collected between 2014 and 2017 through the NoSarC Norwegian Sarcoma Study, the Norwegian Childhood Cancer Biobank, and the Oslo University Hospital Cancer Research Biobank. The team compared them with samples from anonymized healthy individuals, including blood donors, children participating in the Bergen Growth Study, and children visiting a clinic in Bergen. Children with cancer between the ages of two and 19 had substantially more circulating IgG antibodies targeting DNA repair proteins than young adults or older individuals. These antibodies primarily recognized proteins associated with six genes: RAD52, NUMA1, ALKBH7, APBB1, UNG, and MGMT. Although these genes are closely involved in DNA repair, they were not significantly mutated in the cancers studied. This raised the possibility that the proteins could be disrupted by the immune system even when the genes encoding them remained largely intact. Finding these antibodies in children who already had cancer, however, could not establish whether they appeared before the disease or developed in response to it. The researchers therefore examined blood samples collected years earlier from 59 school-age children who participated in two long-term British studies, the Avon Longitudinal Study of Parents and Children and Born in Bradford. Roughly half of these children subsequently developed cancer before turning 30, while the others did not. Comparing the two groups allowed the researchers to investigate whether antibodies targeting DNA repair proteins were present before cancer was diagnosed. “Although this cohort is small, it was the best we could find internationally,” said Myklebost, an emeritus professor of molecular oncology at the University of Bergen. “Even so, we were able to show that indeed, children who later got cancer (on average six years after blood sampling) were about eight times more likely than their healthy peers to have antibodies to at least one core antigen involved in DNA repair.” The findings, published in Frontiers in Immunology , suggest that these antibodies can appear well before cancer develops. Their presence alone does not establish that they cause the disease, however. To explore whether they might actually interfere with DNA repair, the scientists conducted additional experiments using living cells. Those experiments showed that the auto-antibodies could enter cells, particularly during the stage when cells finish growing and prepare to divide. Once inside, the antibodies appeared to concentrate around a cellular structure called the TIGER organelle, where transcription factors and other short-lived but essential proteins are produced and modified. “We showed that many children with various types of cancer have antibodies against some of their own DNA repair proteins. We also demonstrated that such ‘auto-antibodies’ can enter live cells and bind to – and probably inhibit – the activity of these essential proteins,” said corresponding author Myklebost. The researchers propose that antibodies entering a cell or its nucleus could attach to DNA repair proteins and prevent them from working normally. By binding to these proteins, the antibodies might immobilize them or directly interfere with their activity, leaving the cell less capable of correcting genetic damage. Such interference could produce effects resembling those caused by inherited defects in DNA repair genes that increase cancer susceptibility. The difference is that the repair machinery would be impaired by antibodies rather than by mutations in the genes encoding its components. “[These results] together provide a plausible mechanism for increased cellular damage that could lead to cancer development,” concluded the authors. An important question remains unanswered: Why would a child’s immune system begin producing antibodies against proteins needed for DNA repair? “They could be triggered by infections, by crossreacting to some microbial proteins or overstimulation of the immune response, or by some imbalance in immune tolerance,” hypothesized Myklebost. These possibilities remain unconfirmed, but the findings suggest a potential approach to identifying children who may face an increased risk of cancer. If further research establishes that the antibodies contribute to cancer development, screening for them could eventually help identify susceptible children years before diagnosis, potentially allowing earlier detection or even preventive interventions. For now, the researchers are working to determine whether the antibodies directly impair DNA repair and whether that interference can cause cancer. Demonstrating those effects would provide much stronger evidence for the proposed mechanism. “At present we are investigating the effect of patient antibodies on the repair of induced mutations in cultured cells. Ultimately, we hope to clone white blood cells that secrete such auto-antibodies, and test for any cancer-causing effects in mice to definitively prove our hypothesis,” said Myklebost. Reference: “Pathogenic autoantibodies targeting DNA repair proteins are shared by cancer patients and healthy children later diagnosed with cancer” by Anastassia Serguienko, Jeetesh Sharma, Ronas Shakya, Monica Cheng Munthe-Kaas, Kjetil Boye and Ola Myklebost, 25 August 2026, Frontiers in Immunology . title: What to know about cychlorphine, a drug more potent than fentanyl
content: It’s an unfamiliar name that comes up in alerts from state medical examiners, local law enforcement and college campuses: cychlorphine. The synthetic opioid has been linked to at least 122 deaths in the US since July 2025, and in April, the Office of National Drug Control Policy identified it as an “emerging drug threat.” In August, the US Drug Enforcement Administration designated cychlorphine as temporary Schedule I drug, making it illegal in the United States. But experts say they don’t expect it to become as widespread or dangerous a problem as many other illicit opioids. Here’s what to know about cychlorphine. Cychlorphine is from a relatively new class of opioids called orphines that haven’t been used for medicinal purposes in the past, according to Dr. Nabarun Dasgupta, a street drug scientist at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill. Cychlorphine cases are “sporadic” in the United States, he said, appearing significantly less often than fentanyl samples. UNC researchers first detected the drug in the United States in August 2024, Dasgupta said. He noted that his colleagues in Europe had been seeing orphines in 2019 and had been watching for the group of drugs to emerge in the US since then. Cychlorphine showing up in the United States is also a consequence of countries around the world making fentanyl analogs illegal, he said. This has pushed illicit markets to create drugs that are not fentanyl-related but have the same effects on users. “It’s not surprising that it’s showed up,” Dasgupta said. Cychlorphine has been seen in about 25 states across the country, according to Dr. Alex Krotulski, director of toxicology and chemistry at the Center for Forensic Science Research and Education. In the Midwest, including Illinois and Tennessee, the drug has been seen in a powdered form, often mixed alongside fentanyl and heroin. In the South, including Texas, Louisiana and Alabama, cychlorphine has appeared in a pill form. Laboratory-based models show that cychlorphine is more potent than fentanyl, which correlates to what researchers can see in humans, Krotulski said. Due to the potency of the drug, it takes only a small amount to get a bigger effect. Dr. Shravani Durbhakula, director of comprehensive pain service at Vanderbilt University, said that because cychlorphine is an opioid, it works on opioid receptors to cause respiratory depression, which is when people stop breathing or their breathing becomes slowed. Cychlorphine can also cause sedation and euphoria, decreased consciousness and unresponsiveness. Symptoms can be reversed with naloxone, the opioid overdose reversal drug also known as Narcan. In cases Durbhakula has seen, cychlorphine is often combined with other substances, even in counterfeits of Xanax and OxyContin, making the effects more powerful and dangerous. “It’s also been found by itself, so it doesn’t mean that it’s always mixed,” Durbhakula said. “But obviously, if you combine it with other things, it gets even more deadly.” Fentanyl test strips do not detect cychlorphine because they’re different drugs, according to Dr. David Liss, an associate professor of emergency medicine at Washington University. The drug is not on typical tests in hospitals, he said, so they may have to order specialized tests to detect it. “I don’t believe that that there’s any kind of way to test for this on an individual scale,” Liss said. Liss said he also thinks there’s an undercount of cases related to the new compounds, as hospitals cannot identify orphine drugs and it’s not clear whether they’re routinely tested in other labs. Krotulski thinks cychlorphine will “fall off here pretty quickly” because it has been scheduled by the DEA and in China, which is the source for many novel opioids. He predicts that the number of cases will decline, appearing only as one-offs in the future. Still, he said, cychlorphine is just one of at least 100 different opioids that he’s seen appear in the last decade, and he is expecting for new opioids to emerge down the road. “For example, we’re not going to be talking about cyclorphine next October,” Krotulski said. “We’re going to be talking about the new and latest opioids, and there may be three or four until that time.”
